An adult regal jumping spider (Phidippus regius) measures 12–18 mm in body length, with females at the top of that range and males slimmer at the bottom, and that small frame sets the whole feeding equation. A spider that size has a gut roughly the volume of a grain of rice. It cannot store a surplus, so every meal has to be sized to the abdomen in front of you, not to a calendar. Feed it too much and the abdomen distends past the carapace; feed it too little and the abdomen flattens into a deflated wedge within a few days.

From the keeper's diary

I fed a subadult female at 19:40 on a Tuesday, two Hydei and a small cricket, because she had looked thin and I had guests coming and wanted her active. By 21:00 she was hanging from the lid with her abdomen stretched and glossy, and by the next morning she had dropped to the floor of the cube and was dragging her back legs. I had overfed a spider hours before a moult I had not predicted — the abdomen had looked lean because the new exoskeleton was already forming underneath. She moulted badly, lost one leg at the patella, and never took a cricket from the tongs again. The lesson cost me an animal and taught me to weigh the abdomen, not my own impatience, before every feed.

What an adult regal actually eats

Regals are active hunters, not web-waiters, so prey has to move. The staple in my room is live Hydei fruit flies — small, slow, and easy for a 12–18 mm spider to subdue without a struggle that costs it energy. One adult takes roughly three to six Hydei per feeding session, or a single small cricket no longer than the spider's own body length. Variety matters less than size: a prey item wider than the carapace is a wrestling match the spider can lose.

Feed in the evening, when they hunt naturally, and remove anything uneaten within 24 hours. Crickets left in the enclosure will chew on a moulting spider, and that is a real risk, not a hobby myth.

{{affiliate:feeding}}

The mistake I see most is portioning by schedule instead of by abdomen. A plump, rounded abdomen the width of the carapace means the spider is fine for several days. A flat, wrinkled one means feed now. That check takes ten seconds and beats any timetable.

How often to feed an adult

For a mature regal kept at room temperature — call it 22–27 °C, 72–80 °F — I feed every three to five days in summer and every five to seven in winter, when metabolism slows. That is my working range, not a law; keepers online argue for anything from twice weekly to fortnightly, and the honest answer is that it depends on the spider's abdomen and the room's warmth. A gravid female eats more and should. A freshly moulted adult may refuse food for a week and that is normal, not a crisis.

Use this sequence for every feed:

  1. Look at the abdomen from above. Rounded and full: skip this feed.
  2. Flat or wrinkled: offer one prey item, wait, offer a second if the first is taken cleanly.
  3. Stop when the abdomen looks plump, not stretched. Overfeeding risks moult problems and, in my experience, a shorter life.
  4. Log the date and what was taken. A refusal after two sessions is a signal to check temperature and hydration.

Water, and the enclosure it lives in

Spiders do not drink from bowls in any useful way. I mist one corner of the enclosure every second day to 60–70 % relative humidity, which gives them droplets to drink and keeps moulting from going wrong. Ventilation has to stay strong — humid and stuffy is how you get mould and dead spiders.

{{affiliate:habitat}}

An arboreal cube of roughly 20 × 20 × 30 cm suits one adult, with vertical surfaces to climb and a hide at the top where moults happen. Temperature is the variable most keepers ignore: below 20 °C the spider slows, stops eating, and the keeper panics and overfeeds. Warm the room, not a heat mat under the enclosure.

Frequently asked questions

Can I feed an adult regal every day?

You can, but the abdomen tells you not to. Daily feeding of an adult in a warm room produces a stretched abdomen within a week and raises the odds of a bad moult. I feed every three to seven days and let the shape of the spider decide, not the calendar.

My spider refuses food — is it dying?

Usually not. A refusal often means a moult is coming, the room is cool, or the spider is already full. Check temperature and abdomen shape first, offer a single fly in two days, and only start worrying after two clear refusals with a visibly thin abdomen.

Do regals need live food only?

Yes. They hunt by movement, and dead prey is largely ignored. Live Hydei or appropriately small crickets are the practical diet; anything pre-killed tends to sit and spoil, which is a hygiene problem in a humid enclosure.
